nuggets.title: Stale Instance List Routes Traffic to Drained Nodes

scenario.symptoms: After a deploy, 18% of checkout requests return HTTP 503 for 4 minutes. Clients still call pod IPs removed from the registry but cached locally.
scenario.interviewerSetup: SDK caches the full instance list for 30 seconds without push updates. Old pods were SIGTERM'd immediately while the cache TTL had not expired.

incident.headline: Client-side discovery cache continues routing to terminated instances after deploy

agenda.goal: Keep client instance lists fresh with push/watch, jittered TTL, and health-aware routing.
agenda.opener: Right after deploy our error rate spiked because clients kept hitting old pods. How does your service discovery cache stay correct?

evidence.strong: Long-lived watch/stream from registry, versioned service entries, short TTL with jitter, passive health checks on calls, subset selection to limit blast radius.
evidence.adequate: Polling every few seconds without push or health checks.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes the registry is always consulted per request.
misconceptions.challenge: If you cache instances for 30s, what happens in second 5 after a pod dies?

probes: How do clients learn a pod was removed before TTL expires?
What retry strategy avoids hammering a bad instance?
hints: Watch beats poll for fast deploys.
Combine registry events with client-side health.
agenda.referenceFix: Registry watch pushing deltas, aggressive TTL on failures, outlier detection before retry storm.

nuggets.title: Registry Partition Serves Conflicting Instance Sets

scenario.symptoms: Two AZs report different instance counts for payment-service. Some clients see 12 healthy nodes, others see 4, during a network partition between control-plane nodes.
scenario.interviewerSetup: The discovery backend uses a 3-node Raft cluster spanning two regions. A link flap split voters; both sides accepted writes briefly before quorum healed.

incident.headline: Split registry quorum yields divergent service membership during partition

agenda.goal: Run the registry on odd-quorum clusters within one region with clear failover, avoiding cross-region voting splits.
agenda.opener: Clients in two AZs saw different numbers of healthy payment pods during a blip. How is registry state stored and kept consistent?

evidence.strong: Odd-member Raft in single region, automatic leader election, read consistency via quorum, regional failover with explicit promotion, anti-entropy after partition.
evidence.adequate: Multi-region Raft without discussing quorum loss.
evidence.weak: Single registry node with manual backup.

misconceptions.pattern: Treats registry as eventually consistent like DNS with no quorum rules.
misconceptions.challenge: What happens if two leaders accept conflicting registrations?

probes: Where should Raft voters live relative to AZ failures?
How do clients behave when registry is unavailable?
agenda.referenceFix: Regional quorum, stale read avoidance, client fallback to last-good snapshot with health checks.

scenario.symptoms: When 30% of catalog-service pods crash, latency on survivors jumps 5x. Load balancer still sends traffic to dead instances for 90 seconds.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Health checks run every 60s; registry gossip propagates deregistration in two hops averaging 45s. No passive failure detection on the client.

incident.headline: Slow health propagation keeps failed instances in rotation during partial outage

agenda.goal: Detect failures quickly with active health checks, gossip, and client-side outlier ejection.
agenda.opener: Half the pods died but the load balancer kept sending traffic to them for over a minute. How fast should discovery reflect reality?

evidence.strong: Sub-second app health endpoints, registry push on state change, client outlier detection, max connection limits per instance, gradual load shift.
evidence.weak: Only TCP connect checks on long interval.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes registry alone guarantees healthy routing.
misconceptions.challenge: Who tells the registry a process died without graceful deregister?

probes: What happens between crash and deregister?
How do surviving pods avoid overload?
hints: Active health checks should be faster than user timeouts.
Clients can eject bad endpoints immediately.
agenda.referenceFix: Fast health checks, push deregister, client-side outlier detection and retry on other instances.

nuggets.title: Aggressive Outlier Ejection Empties the Load Balancer Pool

scenario.symptoms: During a downstream DB slowdown, the mesh ejects every recommendation-service instance within 30 seconds. The service appears entirely unavailable despite pods running.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Outlier detection marks instances bad after 5 consecutive 500ms timeouts with no minimum pool size. All instances share the same dependency latency.

incident.headline: Outlier detection confuses systemic dependency failure with bad instances

agenda.goal: Tune outlier ejection with minimum healthy percentage, success-rate windows, and distinction from global outages.
agenda.opener: Our mesh ejected every instance during a database slowdown and the service went fully dark. How should outlier detection behave?

evidence.strong: Ejection thresholds relative to cluster average, max ejection percent, panic mode when too few hosts remain, distinguish client vs server errors, circuit break dependency not all pods.
evidence.adequate: Fixed consecutive error count without pool floor.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes if all instances fail the same way, ejecting them helps.
misconceptions.challenge: Where will traffic go if every host is ejected?

probes: When should you stop ejecting instances?
How do you detect a shared dependency failure?
agenda.referenceFix: Outlier detection with max ejection ratio, panic threshold, upstream circuit breaker on DB.

nuggets.title: Long DNS TTL Serves IPs After Kubernetes Rollout

scenario.symptoms: External partners hitting api.example.com via DNS still connect to decommissioned load balancer IPs 20 minutes after cutover.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Legacy clients use DNS SRV with TTL 1800s. Kubernetes service changed external IP but DNS updates propagated slowly at resolvers.

incident.headline: High DNS TTL delays discovery of new endpoints for external callers

agenda.goal: Integrate DNS with discovery using low TTL for volatile names, dual-stack cutover, and SRV/HTTP alternatives where needed.
agenda.opener: Partners still hit our old load balancer IP long after we migrated. How does DNS fit your discovery story for external clients?

evidence.strong: Low TTL for dynamic records, gradual traffic shift with both IPs live, alias to stable anycast front door, document resolver behavior, prefer service mesh or API gateway stable hostname.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes updating authoritative DNS instantly changes all clients.
misconceptions.challenge: What about resolvers that cache for the full TTL?

probes: What TTL is appropriate for internal vs external names?
How do you run a zero-downtime IP migration?
hints: Run old and new in parallel during TTL window.
Stable anycast name hides backend IP churn.
agenda.referenceFix: Short TTL, overlap period with both endpoints, monitor stale resolver caches.
